catalog_citation: Keegan, John M. & Kodé Koutou. 2015. Dictionary of Na: Na-French, French-Na, with Introduction in English. First edition, December 2015. Cuenca: Morkeg Books (The Sara-Bagirmi Languages Project). PDF from morkegbooks.com, 332 pp.
catalog_locator: English grammatical introduction, sec. 1.2 Vowel Length and sec. 1.3 Tone (pp. v-vi); whole PDF searched for 'stress' (0 hits) and 'accent' (no prosodic uses)
catalog_quote: 1.3 Tone Like the Sara Languages, Na has three level tones: high, mid and low: (3) ká ‘so that, for’ kō ‘already’ ɓà ‘rainy season’ Tone-bearing phonemes are vowels and sonorant consonants when they are in final position. When a morpheme contains a sequence of identical vowels with distinct tones, or when a sonorant consonant closes a syllable, complex tones occur: (4) kàā ‘toad’ nàw ‘to love’ ... Of the nine possible combinations, Mid-Low is not found. High-Low, which is very rare in the Sara languages with native morphemes, is common in Na, and is frequently used in verb conjugations. While Mid-Mid and Low-Low are common in Na, as they are in the Sara Languages, High-High tone, also common in the Sara languages, is rare in Na.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage (sec. 1.3 Tone, pp. v-vi) is verbatim in the publisher PDF we hold/text at the stated locator; 'stress' has 0 hits in the 330-page text and 'accent' none prosodic, as the record says. (2) Deciding source: a 2015 grammar sketch (65-pp introduction to a dictionary) by the family specialist John Keegan with a native-speaker co-author, SIL-reviewed; it states a three-level lexical tone system positively and never mentions stress, so classification tonal, domain not stated by the source is the right reading. (3) Against Glottolog's list, the held work (2014/2015 editions) is the newest and fullest description; the only other description is Fédry & Danay 1981, a 146-pp CELS pedagogical manual in print only; the Ngambay item is misattached; no phonology article, instrumental study, dissertation or JIPA illustration of Na appears in Glottolog, on the publisher's project page, or in Keeg

sources.note: Group-level claim only: the western SBB branch (which includes Na via the 'sara' subgroup, Tableau 3) went from 2 to 3 distinctive tone heights; Na appears as 3 tone-marked forms (bàrū, òyō, ìtà).

tone.quote: Dans le cas particulier des langues SBB, deux domaines sont révélateurs d’innovations partagées : les systèmes tonals et le lexique. Le passage de deux à trois hauteurs tonales distinctives (et les correspondances qui en résultent dans le domaine de la morphologie verbale) caractérise notamment la branche des langues ‘occidentales’ (*OCC), qui s’est solidairement détachée des autres langues avant de se diversifier à son tour. ... L’important sous-groupe des langues ‘sara’ justifie à lui seul l’identification d’un système tardif *SARA dont ces dernières sont issues.
tone.locator: §3 Filiation des langues SBB, author-version p. 2; Na placed under *SARA within *OCC in Tableau 3, p. 8
tone.translation: In the particular case of the SBB languages, two domains reveal shared innovations: the tone systems and the lexicon. The passage from two to three distinctive tone heights (and the resulting correspondences in verbal morphology) characterises in particular the branch of 'western' languages (*OCC), which split off together from the other languages before diversifying in turn. ... The large 'sara' subgroup by itself justifies identifying a later system *SARA from which these derive.
tone.summary: Group-level claim only: the western SBB branch (which includes Na via the 'sara' subgroup, Tableau 3) went from 2 to 3 distinctive tone heights; Na appears as 3 tone-marked forms (bàrū, òyō, ìtà).

Présentation des langues sara-bongo-baguirmiennes (introductory document, 649 Ko PDF). Villejuif/Paris: CNRS-LLACAN. Originally athttp://sumale.vjf.cnrs.fr/SBB/,nowhttps://llacan.cnrs.fr/SBB/.
sources.note: Each cognate series carries one or more tonal correspondence formulae identified at three successive historical levels (*SBB, *OCC, *SARA); nominal and verbal series are kept apart because their tonal correspondences diverge; the 'western' (*OCC) system, to which na belongs, is characterised by the development of a third tone register; na forms are cited with tone marks throughout the series. It is a comparative tool, not a description of Na's synchronic tone system.
